notes.short: God's “eyes”: His watchful care for the faithful
notes.about: Hanani tells Asa that the LORD's eyes roam over all the earth. Eyes are spoken of God to show that He watches over all and looks for every chance to help those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him. Asa had trusted the king of Aram instead.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.words: the eyes of the LORD roam to and fro
figure.means: the LORD's watchful care and favour, ready to help those devoted to Him

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anthropopatheia: eyes are given to God for His grace and favour. Henry reads them as His providence, which sees all and directs His hand. Ball (Ellicott) says the Lord is ever watching for times to help the faithful, and Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says He uses every opportunity to succour those devoted to Him.

cites.quote: Eyes are used of God’s grace and favour. ... “The eyes of the Jehovah thy God, are always upon it”: i.e., regarding the Land with Divine benevolence. So 1Ki 9:3. 2Ch 16:9.

cites.quote: That God governs the world in infinite wisdom, and the creatures, and all their actions, are continually under his eye. The eye of Providence is quick-sighted ... and his eye directs his hand, and the arm of his power; for he shows himself strong.
The Lord is ceaselessly watchful for occasions of helping the faithful.

cites.quote: i.e., for Jahve, who looks forth over all the earth, uses every opportunity wonderfully to succour those who are piously devoted to Him.

notes.short: With us, with him, then with him, with us
notes.about: Hezekiah says “with us” and then “with him,” and turns the words back the other way: “With him is only the arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God.” The reversal sets the two sides against each other: the king of Assyria, with only the arm of flesh, and Judah, with the LORD.

figure.name: Antimetabole
figure.words: With him is only the arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God
figure.means: the LORD, who is with Judah, set against the arm of flesh that is with the king of Assyria

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists these verses under Antimetabole, or Counterchange, words repeated in reverse order to oppose one thing to another, and sets them out a b b a: more with us, than with him; with him an arm of flesh, but with us the Lord our God.
notes.limit: The note is about how the words are set out.

cites.quote: This figure repeats the word or words in a reverse order, for the purpose of opposing one thing to another, or of contrasting two or more things. ... a There be more with us b than with him; b With him is an arm of flesh, a but with us is the Lord our God.
